title: France’s Halley Production Boards Thriller ‘Carro Seco,’ About Killer Who Targets Unscrupulous Barcelona Real Estate Speculators (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Paris-based Halley Production has boarded Javier Polo’s feature film thriller project “Carro Seco” (“Carreau”), showcased at the upcoming Iberseries
body:
Paris-based Halley Production has boarded Javier Polo’s feature film thriller project “Carro Seco” (“Carreau”), showcased at the upcoming Iberseries & Platino Industria’s Co-Production and Financing Forum in Madrid.

	Halley Production is partnering on “Carro Seco” with València-based Los Hermanos Polo Films, which Polo runs with brother Guillermo Polo, and Lastcrit in Barcelona.


	Set in a Barcelona suffocated by the housing crisis and evictions, the contemporary urban thriller turns on an eccentric serial killer who executes wealthy real estate speculators using heavy metal pétanque balls. His targets are ruthless property owners who profit from the silent tragedy of housing displacement and eviction.
	

	Dressed like a vintage pétanque player, the vigilante is driven by the social impact of gentrification. Casting himself as a housing Robin Hood, he justifies his crimes as acts committed for the common good.

	As two detectives navigate the investigation, public opinion splits between viewing the murderer as a heroic housing vigilante or a psychopath.

	“‘Carro Seco’ uses the tension of a psychological thriller to address one of today’s most urgent social conflicts: silent evictions and real estate speculation,” says Polo. “What sets it apart is the contrast between that social nightmare and a unique, ritualistic iconography; turning an innocent neighborhood sport like pétanque into a deadly weapon accompanied by French chanson. It is a film that challenges the viewer with an uncomfortable moral dilemma about justice, boundaries, and empathy.”
	

	Halley Production’s international co-productions include such cross-border hits as Javier Fesser’s 2018 crowd-pleaser “Champions,” Manuel Gómez Pereira’s 2025 Goya-winning Spanish hit “The Dinner” and the forthcoming drama “Primo Viaggio.”

	“From our very first meeting with Javier Polo, my associate and producer Corentin Koskas and I felt that ‘Carreau’ called for a genuinely organic Spanish-French co-production. Pétanque is part of a shared culture on both sides of the border and it provides the starting point for an original social thriller,” said Andrea Marcelli, a partner at Halley Production, which has backed multiple Spanish films in the past, including Icíar Bollaín’s ‘Rosa’s Wedding,” Javier Fesser’s “Champions” and “Ma Ma” by Julio Medem. 

	He added: “At the same time, the film’s portrait of Barcelona’s transformation through gentrification speaks just as powerfully to Paris and to so many other European cities. The French dimension is woven into the film’s very fabric, making this co-production a creative necessity. This is truly a film born at the crossroads of our two countries, with a clear ambition to reach audiences internationally.”

	“‘Carro Seco’ is, by nature, an organic and logical co-production with France given its core story elements, and Halley’s extensive expertise in French-Spanish partnerships makes them the perfect partner to bring this film to life,” said producer Victoria Pérez de la Cruz of Los Hermanos Polo Films. Also producing are Javier Polo, Guillermo Polo, Víctor Cuadros and Guillem Moreno.

	“Carro Seco” was written by María Mínguez, co-creator of the Fesser-directed Disney+ original Spanish comedy series “Shared Custody,” and Merli Marlowe, who co-wrote Javier Polo’s comedy documentary “The Mystery of the Pink Flamingo.” Javier Polo’s works also include the comedy “Pet Peeves” and the music documentary “Europe in 8 Bits.”

	The producers will be attending Iberseries & Platino Industria with the aim of finding key partners to assist in the film’s international rollout. 

	“Carro Seco” is aimed for a 2027 shoot. The cast has yet to be announced.

	Anna Marie de la Fuente contributed to this article. 



	

					Javier Polo

title: ‘The Inbetweeners’ Original Lead Cast Confirmed for Netflix Reunion Movie as Production Kicks Off in U.K.
description: The original lead cast of cult Brit teen comedy series “The Inbetweeners” are officially back for the upcoming reunion movie at Netflix, which the s
body:
The original lead cast of cult Brit teen comedy series “The Inbetweeners” are officially back for the upcoming reunion movie at Netflix, which the streamer has confirmed is now in production. 

	First reported last month, the new film has now been given the title “Inbetweeners 3,” following on from the hit show’s two record-breaking spin-off features. 

	Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles as Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper, with “The Inbetweeners” creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris returning to write and direct the film.
	

	“It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans,” said the directors. 

	In a video announcing the start of production, the four main characters are seen getting into the famous 1996 Fiat Cinqeucento Hawaii car from the second season, still missing a door and sporting a sticker that says “Honk if You Want a Blowjob.”



	“The Inbetweeners 3” will be produced by Claire Jones alongside Banijay’s Patrick Holland and Fudge Park Production’s Mark Lesbirel. Caroline Levy, Caroline Leddy, Phil Gilbert, Suzanne Knight, Tom Jordan, Farhana Bhula (for Film4), Morris and Beesley will serve as executive producers.

	Originally broadcast on E4 in the U.K. between 2008 and 2010, “The Inbetweeners” followed the misadventures of suburban teenager MacKenzie (Bird) and his friends Cooper (Thomas), Sutherland (Harrison) and Cartwright (Buckley) at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life, friendship, male bonding, lad culture and failed sexual encounters. It was originally conceived as a more realistic counterpoint to fellow hit Brit teen show “Skins.”
	

	After three seasons, two hit movies followed, released in 2011 and 2014 respectively. The first set a record for the biggest opening weekend for a U.K. comedy at the time of its release while the sequel also broke box office records.

	The news comes less than a year after rights holders Banijay U.K. revealed that it had struck a deal with Morris and Beesley and their Fudge Park Productions that, at the time, they said “paves the way for the return of the hit comedy title.”

schema.headline: ‘The Inbetweeners’ Original Lead Cast Confirmed for Netflix Reunion Movie as Production Kicks Off in U.K.

title: ‘Strawberry and Chocolate’ Star Jorge Perugorría and Brazil’s Thiago Lacerda Lead Havana-Set ‘Hotel Nacional’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Cuba’s Jorge Perugorría, best known for his lead role in the iconic Oscar-nominated Cuban classic “Strawberry and Chocolate” (“Fresa y Chocolate”),
body:
Cuba’s Jorge Perugorría, best known for his lead role in the iconic Oscar-nominated Cuban classic “Strawberry and Chocolate” (“Fresa y Chocolate”), has been cast in the upcoming film, “Hotel Nacional” which participates in the Iberseries & Platino Industria Co-Production and Financing Forum.

	He plays opposite Brazilian star Thiago Lacerda, (“Seven Women”) who plays a grieving man who goes to Havana in a bid to reconnect with the roots of his recently deceased Cuban wife.
	

	He meets Pilar, a Spanish doctor, who’s in the Cuban capital for a conference, hoping to escape the routine of her life in Madrid. At the bar of the emblematic Hotel Nacional, their paths cross – and they find an unlikely confidant in Rubén (Perugorría), a veteran Cuban bartender who introduces them to a forgotten cocktail.


	As Bruno and Pilar grow closer, they wander the streets of Havana and the corridors of the hotel they share, drinking, talking, and confronting the ghosts that haunt them—through alcohol, guilt, and each other.

	It will be helmed by writer, director and producer Diego Corsini (“Adiós Madrid”) in his eighth feature film outing as a director.

	“Rubén is a 60-year-old Cuban who has lived his entire life in Havana and has spent more than 30 years as the bartender at the Hotel Nacional’s bar. With his family scattered since his children moved abroad, his work is the only thing that distracts him from his loneliness, ever since his wife passed away a few years ago,” Corsini explained.

	He added: “At the bar, he has his ‘occasional friends’—the tourists staying at the hotel, with whom he often manages to have deep conversations, frequently becoming a confidant. The arrival of Bruno and Pilar will leave a lasting mark on him, not only because of the bond they will gradually develop, but also because of the Brazilian’s story, which ultimately contains a hidden element that will be revealed toward the end of the film.”
	

	“He is a very sociable, warm, and calm man, with extensive knowledge of classic cocktails and traditional drinks, many of which have been forgotten in the face of newer trends. The cocktail ‘Between the Sheets’ will play a key role in the connection he forms with Bruno and Pilar,” he told Variety.

	Asked about the difficulties in shooting in Havana given its economic crisis, he remained hopeful. “The situation is very complicated, and we hope that things will return to normal soon. Hopefully, this will happen before we begin filming. In any case, the Cuban people have an enormous and wonderful capacity for adaptation and creativity.” He has targeted early next year to begin shooting the drama.

	“Alternative energy sources, including solar power, as well as electric vehicles, have already been making significant progress and growing considerably. So, one way or another, we are confident and reassured that we will be able to successfully carry out the portion of the shoot that takes place in Cuba.”

	And whether shooting at the famous Hotel Nacional would pose a challenge, he was also positive. “Every iconic location comes with its own challenges, and the Hotel Nacional is no exception. That said, having our Cuban partners at i4films, with their extensive experience and track record, gives us confidence that we will be able to make it happen. This is further reinforced by the official support of ICAIC (the Cuban Institute of Cinematographic Art and Industry), as well as the fact that films have already been shot there in the past.”

	He added: “The Hotel is essentially another character in the film—and it is the title of the film itself. For that reason, we are confident that the hotel’s management will not only allow us to shoot there, but will also enthusiastically support the production.”

	The film is lead produced by Cinescalas, Spain along with TVZero, Brazil and i4films.

	Co-founded by Corsini and Mariana Cangas, Cinescalas has produced close to 20 feature films, both fiction and documentary, in the past two decades. Among its credits, aside from “Adios Madrid,” are “Pasaje de Vida,” “Lo que nunca nos dijimos” co-produced with Mexico, “Candy Bar,” coproduced with Venezuela, “Solo el Amor,” on Netflix exclusively for 5 years, “El Encanto” and “Punto de no Retorno,” among others.
	

	The sixth edition of Iberseries & Platino Industria takes place from Sept. 29 to Oct. 2.

title: ‘Into the Breach’ Review: Star-Studded British Theater Doc Needs More Time to Serve Its Sprawling Subject Matter
description: The self-professed “story of a theatrical revolution and how it shaped a nation,” Freddie Fox’s documentary “Into the Breach” attempts to chronicle
body:
The self-professed “story of a theatrical revolution and how it shaped a nation,” Freddie Fox’s documentary “Into the Breach” attempts to chronicle the impact that British theater has exerted on art, culture and politics over the last century. Assembling a roundtable of acting legends that includes Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Gary Oldman and co-producer Kenneth Branagh, Fox injects anecdotes and insights into a history lesson written by Richard Fullerton that, for better or worse, invites more curiosity than it satisfies. Suffice it to say that these are performers who are not only full of great stories but know how to tell one. Yet the film’s obligation to historical detail renders slightly bland what could have been a tasty trip through 20th-century theater.
	

	Backtracking to the beginning of the 1900s, Fox catalogues the major players who defined, and in many cases changed, British theater: Lilian Baylis, Derek Jacobi, John Gielgud, Paul Robeson, Claire Bloom, Laurence Olivier, Joan Plowright, Richard Burton — the list is considerable. Baylis, a producer and manager, pioneered Shakespeare at the Old Vic theatre in Waterloo, the eventual site of London’s storied National Theatre. Among the performers who became famous on its stage were Gielgud (an eventual EGOT winner) and Olivier, as well as Michael Redgrave and Ralph Richardson. Later came theater director Peter Hall, impresario Andrew Lloyd Webber and performers such as Peter O’Toole, Helen Mirren and Stephen Rea.


	As Fox charts their accomplishments, the panel looks back at their professional and personal intersections with them, from compliments to rebuffs. As necessary as the broader context may be, it’s the personal stories, big and small, that resonate and reveal the most. Gielgud was arrested in 1953 for homosexuality at a time when it was illegal in Britain, and he feared that it would ruin his career; his transgression was reported by the press, and it took the support of his costar Sybil Thorndike to help him go out on stage that night. Rather than a rebuke, Gielgud received a standing ovation, highlighting the almost transcendent affection that some of these performers generated from their fans. Meanwhile, despite treating Hopkins with cheeky kindness early in the future Oscar winner’s stage career, Olivier earned a reputation for cruelty.
	

	Further, rivalries like the one between the British theater community’s two pillars, the National Theatre and the Royal Shakespeare Company, could probably provide enough material for a film on its own. While the National Theatre Company, founded by Olivier, focused heavily on classic material, the RSC, created by Peter Hall, took chances on a wide variety of challenging contemporary and even avant-garde material. Hall being named director of the National Theatre in 1973 was a devasting blow to Olivier, but the film moves on fairly quickly in order to ensure it covers what is, admittedly, a lot of material. Plowright’s adulation of her husband Olivier is sweetly affecting, but let’s hear more about the many young actors, themselves now household names, whom he dismissed or dressed down in their nascent years.

	Fox traces the community’s sociocultural impact with moderate efficacy — not just the introduction of plays like John Osborne’s “Look Back in Anger,” which marked a shift in focus on working-class characters, but the campaigning and promoting for gay rights by figures like Ian McKellen. Former prime minister John Major, for example, recounts how a meeting with McKellen over the issue permanently changed his perspective, leading to new legislation. (McKellen, on the other hand, remembers identifying that Major was the only straight person in the room where they met, even if his counterpart wasn’t aware.) Stephen Rea’s Irish acting troupe, meanwhile, explored the complexities of the Troubles in their work, spotlighting the conflict in new ways. And British theater was a receptive community for African American actor Paul Robeson to demonstrate his incomparable stage presence after he struggled to find work in the U.S.

	Extraordinarily, but perhaps unsurprisingly, many of the roundtable participants are able to recall meaty chunks of dialogue from plays they did decades before, and cheerfully deliver them here to the admiration of their colleagues — who in several cases were present to witness their original performances. Upon remembering Hopkins playing Lambert LaRue in “Pravda,” a role that reportedly helped him land the part of Hannibal Lecter in “The Silence of the Lambs,” Oldman says, “I knew I was in the presence of the one of the greatest performers of the 20th century.” With a laugh, Oldman also rhapsodizes about his acting heroes all being drunks, but the net result of the conversation is a thumbnail master class in inspiration and perspiration, about how these individuals became great actors.
	

	Though the film provides an overview of a century in this community and the cultural evolution of an art form, overall that’s all it can do given its single-serving running time. Give us a docuseries or an extended cut, please: There are so many different threads to follow – past or present — that, again, probably deserve their own films, or at least more of a direct focus. Thatcherism and its devastating effect on the theater community at the same time as the rise of Lloyd Webber-style spectacle certainly merits a more incisive look than it receives here. On top of the history itself, not simply sitting a camera in front of these acting legends — including some no longer around like Plowright — to hear as many stories as they would share about their life and work feels a bit like a missed opportunity. Ultimately, “Into the Breach” covers a topic of undeniable importance. But it doesn’t go into it deeply enough.

schema.headline: ‘Into the Breach’ Review: Star-Studded British Theater Doc Needs More Time to Serve Its Sprawling Subject Matter

title: Lav Diaz on the Hunt for Truth in ‘An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman,’ Third Chapter of His Acclaimed Hermes Trilogy (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Venice Golden Lion winner Lav Diaz (“The Woman Who Left”), who returns to the Lido this week with the Venice Open selection “Let Us Through, Dear An
body:
Venice Golden Lion winner Lav Diaz (“The Woman Who Left”), who returns to the Lido this week with the Venice Open selection “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” (Makikiraan Po), is in post-production on “An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman.” The Filipino auteur presented the film during the Venice Gap-Financing Market, which took place Sept. 4 – 6.

	The third installment of the director’s “Hermes Trilogy,” the Lisbon-set drama follows Lieutenant Ines Horta — described as “one of the finest detectives in the city” — as she investigates a mystery with the help of Sergeant Mariana Moura. Hoping for information from Filippino Lieutenant Hermes Papauran that never arrives, she decides to leave Mariana to deal with the case, putting her life in danger in the process.
	

	“An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman” is produced by Jean-Christophe Simon for Films Boutique and co-produced by Epic Media and Rosa Filmes, with the support of ARTE, Bord Cadre and Sovereign Films. It’s written and directed by Diaz and stars Monica Calle, Ana Vilela Da Costa and John Lloyd Cruz.


	The film picks up the thread of Diaz’s previous features, “When the Waves Are Gone” (2020) and “Essential Truths of the Lake” (2023), both of which premiered at the Locarno Film Festival and followed the obsessive, disillusioned Lt. Papauran, billed as “arguably the greatest Filipino investigator ever,” played memorably by Cruz.  

	Though “Sadness” chronicles an investigation led by Portuguese Lt. Horta, the specter of the Filipino detective — described by Variety’s Peter Debruge in his “Essential Truths” review as “a good cop in a corrupt country” — still looms large. 
	

	“Although the focus of this film is now on the brilliant Portuguese investigator Ines Horta, the spirit of Lt. Hermes Papauran is still very present in it,” Diaz told Variety. “They are friends and colleagues, and they share the same idealism in the conduct of their profession. They are for truth. They are obsessed with the truth. They classify truth the way punctuation mark stops a word or ends a sentence; it must not go beyond period. It stops there.”

	The director described both investigators as “deeply conflicted beings, restless and battered souls,” whose “inner turmoils are channeled in their probing of hardcore cases.” “They are both outliers in the system they’re working for as they know the dysfunctions of it, but they work around it, oftentimes, carrying their tasks on their own terms, as they don’t trust the orthodoxies of investigations,” Diaz said.

	Like many detective stories that came before it, the Hermes Trilogy gnaws at existential questions as much as the simple mechanics of a classic whodunit; as the director puts it: “The great investigator, the obsessive visionary, aims for the mystery of existence.” 

	Would Diaz apply the same distinction to filmmakers?

	“In the case of the filmmaker as a visionary, it simply has to do with a grasp of reality, that deep understanding of life. It’s never on the technical side, it’s never about money, the budget, but more on the perspective realm,” he said. “The visionary filmmaker is trying to crack the mystery of existence. Why is there sadness? Why is there passion? Why am I evil? Why did I fuck my neighbor’s wife? 

	“The visionary filmmaker is obsessed with the idea of responsibility — what his cinema can do for humanity’s survival,” he continued. “Ultimately, the visionary filmmaker seeks only the truth. And that’s humility.”

	Ten years after winning the Golden Lion with “The Woman Who Left,” Diaz is in Venice with “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors,” a period drama set in the late 16th century and early 17th century, when Spanish forces under Miguel Lopez de Legazpi consolidated colonial rule 44 years after Magellan first landed in the archipelago. “It is an essential part of my continuing studies and dissection of my people’s struggle, or simply trying to understand the history of the Philippines,” Diaz said.
	

	The film arrives one year after Diaz’s “Magellan,” starring Gael García Bernal as the Portuguese explorer, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival.

schema.headline: Lav Diaz on the Hunt for Truth in ‘An Entry Into the Sadness of a Portuguese Woman,’ Third Chapter of His Acclaimed Hermes Trilogy (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Tsai Ming-liang on Venice and San Sebastian Title ‘Dust,’ Slowness as Rebellion and Life With Lee Kang-sheng
description: A barefoot monk in a red robe walks the length of San Sebastian’s La Concha, pauses beneath the concrete rooms of Chillida Leku and stands before th
body:
A barefoot monk in a red robe walks the length of San Sebastian’s La Concha, pauses beneath the concrete rooms of Chillida Leku and stands before the crashing wall of the Peine del Viento. He is Tsai Ming-liang‘s Walker, and in “Dust,” the 11th installment of the director’s “Walker” series, his slow procession moves through Spain for the first time. 

	The film debuts at the Venice Film Festival, then moves to the San Sebastian Film Festival.
	

	Produced by Vitrine Filmes and Homegreen Films, with backing from the Basque regional government’s culture and language department, the Taiwan Public Television Service Foundation and Tabakalera, “Dust” continues a project Tsai launched in 2012 built around a single recurring image: Lee Kang-sheng walking in near-stillness through unfamiliar cities, his body tracing how a place is felt and moved through over time.


	Tsai traces the whole project back to a stage production more than a decade ago, where a slow-walking performance by Lee left a lasting mark on him. “At the time, I had grown tired of making narrative films, and Lee’s slow walk gave me the idea of making something non-narrative, a form of pure visual expression,” he says. “The way he walks is extraordinarily beautiful, and the idea of ‘slowness’ itself has great power.” What still strikes him, after 15 years of filming the same gesture, is Lee’s physical control: “He is still able to maintain the same power he had at the very beginning.”

	Spain entered the picture through a co-production partner. Tsai says he scouted San Sebastian twice before settling on it, taken with the city itself but even more with what surrounded it: “Basque stone houses, an abandoned mining tunnel, the tremendous force of the waves crashing against the Peine del Viento, the sound of church bells surrounding San Sebastian and the face of an elderly Basque farmer.”
	

	That patience is, for Tsai, the whole point of the exercise. Cinema, he argues, has trained audiences to treat images as information to be processed rather than looked at. “Slowness may simply be a method: it allows you to become quiet, to really look and to feel — to gaze at a face, an object, an event,” he says. “Slowness, in fact, is also a form of rebellion.”

	The series has by now carried the Walker from Taipei and Hong Kong through two further shorts shot at a Yunlin exhibition space, on to Kuching, Malaysia; Marseille, France; Tokyo; the Taiwan‘s Yilan coast; Paris; and Washington, D.C., before this latest journey to San Sebastian, and Tsai describes him as a kind of instrument for reading a place. Every city, he says, carries its own atmosphere and pace, and Lee’s shaved head, bare feet and red robe throw that character into relief. In San Sebastian, what caught him was the light: “The sunlight constantly shifting between brightness and shadow, falling across enormous sculptures, forests, streets, pedestrians and the Walker’s red robe. It is very beautiful.”

	Underneath the travelogue is a much longer collaboration. Tsai and Lee have worked together for more than 30 years, and the director speaks of the series as something closer to a document of aging than a formal experiment. “We have watched Lee Kang-Sheng’s body, appearance, and even his skin change,” he says. “Only through looking at someone over a long period of time can the reality of a life be fully revealed. To have been able to keep filming Lee Kang-Sheng is the greatest gift heaven has given me.”

	Venice has bookended Tsai’s career in its own way. “Vive L’Amour” won the Golden Lion there in 1994; “Dust” returns him to the festival with a film that shares almost nothing with it formally. Tsai frames the distance between the two less as a rupture than as an ongoing argument with the medium itself. Some assume he stopped making films, he says, simply because he stopped making the kind audiences expected: “In fact, I have never stopped making films. I have been searching for the possibilities of cinema: what else can cinema express, besides telling stories?” He questions whether the theater itself has grown too conservative a container: “It should be able to contain all kinds of films, not only narrative films or documentaries. The ‘Walker’ series is clearly neither fiction nor documentary. It is simply a form of cinema, and it deserves to be seen in a cinema.”
	

	He’s less pessimistic about audiences than that argument might suggest. Tsai splits viewers into two camps — one seeking pure entertainment, another open to work that asks more of them — and says the second group hasn’t shrunk. “My films are screened in cities all over the world, and I have found that more and more young people are coming to see them.”

	Working with a largely new Spanish crew, he says, didn’t require him to change anything. Tsai has long mixed his longtime Taiwanese team with international crews and film students, and this production was no exception: “I was very satisfied with the Spanish team this time, especially the two cinematographers. I really liked the way they handled the images.”

	The series isn’t finished with him yet. The next “Walker” film will take him to Jeonju, Korea, on an invitation from the Jeonju Intl. Film Festival, and Tsai is untroubled by questions about where the project ends. “I think it will end only when either Lee Kang-Sheng or I am no longer here,” he says.

	Beyond “Walker,” his ambitions have narrowed rather than faded. “I am getting older now, and I do not have the same energy I once had,” he says. “The one thing I still very much hope to do is to work once more with all the actors I have collaborated with over the years. Perhaps I will make one more narrative film that is not really a narrative film.”

	Three decades after his Golden Lion, Tsai returns to Venice with a film that has no plot, no dialogue and, by his own account, no interest in changing that.

schema.headline: Tsai Ming-liang on Venice and San Sebastian Title ‘Dust,’ Slowness as Rebellion and Life With Lee Kang-sheng

title: Arte France’s ‘Tax Me (If You Can)’ Sells to Multiple Territories: ‘Getting Rich People to Talk About Money Was Tough,’ Says Director (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Paris-based The Party Film Sales, attached to Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab” and Cannes Un Certain Regard winner “Congo Boy,” has inked m
body:
Paris-based The Party Film Sales, attached to Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab” and Cannes Un Certain Regard winner “Congo Boy,” has inked multiple deals on the French documentary “Tax Me (If You Can),” helmed by Thomas Lafarge (“The World According to Amazon,” “In the Murky Waters of BNP Paribas”). 

	New pubcasters on board the Little Big Story production include RTVE in Spain, RTS in Switzerland, RTV in Slovenia and YLE in Finland. The deals were announced on the eve of the French TV confab Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, and ahead of the documentary’s national launch on Arte France’s streamer arte.tv Sept. 8 and ARTE channel Sept. 14. 
	

	“Managing to secure leading European broadcasters so quickly, ahead of the first broadcast, is a very encouraging sign, particularly in the current challenging market where public broadcasters and their funding are facing significant pressure,” said The Party Film Sales’ Estelle de Araujo, co-head of international sales. 

	Describing Thomas Lafarge’s film as “an economic investigation, a documentary tackling some crucial and current political issues,” De Araujo also said “the fact that broadcasters have chosen to air it so fast is therefore an encouraging editorial and political signal. It shows a real appetite for these topics from the decision-makers who have a key role to play in bringing them to wider audiences.”

	Shopped as a 52 minute-feature or a two-parter of 45 minutes, “Tax Me (If You Can!)” is the latest dive into the financial clout of the power-players of this world from investigative journalist and filmmaker Thomas Lafarge, co-director with Adrien Pinon of “The World According to Amazon” and “In the Murky Water of BNP Paribas” with Xavier Harel. 
	

	In his new film, the 38-year-old helmer turns on the power of money and potential ways of changing the rules of the games. He investigates both how the ultra-rich have seen their fortunes soar in the last 20 years, while the “trickle-down” economics theory promoted by U.S. economist Arthur Laffer has been gaining momentum as has the emerging “tax the rich” movement led by French economist Gabriel Zucman and backed by a handful of millionaires including Abigail Disney. 

	Lafarge said reading in the media about multi-millionaires calling for higher taxes was what first caught his attention, together with Olivier Lamour who came up with the idea, and producer Valérie Montmartin. “The traditional approach would have been to reach out to Oxfam or Attac, which have been working on these issues for decades, but as Chuck Collins puts it so well in the film, “A dog biting a man is no surprise, but a man biting a dog – that’s news!” And ultra-rich people asking to be taxed is a man bites dog story,” Lafarge said. 

	Then accessing Zucman was a mix of intuition and luck. “I’d been familiar with this economist’s work for a long time, and when I approached his team, they told me to come to Washington for the G20. They told me that something interesting was going to happen. But I had no idea that it would be the starting point for an international campaign on taxing billionaires, which is now part of the public debate in France, the U.K., Sweden, and the United States.”

	However, getting the uber-rich to actually open up about their wealth was the biggest challenge. 

	“People often think that wealthy French people have a problem talking about money. But in reality, wealthy people all over the world have a problem talking about money. Even those who want to pay more taxes. They know they’re exposing themselves to risks, and they’re very cautious,” Lafarge said. With this film, De Araujo hopes issues such as inequality, the concentration of wealth, and the debate around fair taxation of the ultra-rich “will have a strong global resonance.” 

	At this week’s Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, the sales executive aims to lock new deals from partners who have already expressed interest, especially from the Nordics, Japan, Portugal, Eastern Europe, and in the rest of the world. 
	

	“Tax Me (If You Can!)” was produced by Little Big Story (“Nicole Kidman, Eyes Wide Open,” “Welded Together”) in co-production with Arte France, in association with Public Sénat, and support from the CNC, PROCIREP, Société des Producteurs, ANGOA, and Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes Region.

	The Unifrance Rendez-Vous market runs Sept-7-10 in Le Havre, Normandy.

title: Gaza Cinema Academy Launches at Venice Film Festival
description: A group of prominent Palestinian, Arab and international filmmakers and industry professionals on Monday launched the Gaza Cinema Academy at the Ven
body:
A group of prominent Palestinian, Arab and international filmmakers and industry professionals on Monday launched the Gaza Cinema Academy at the Venice Film Festival. The new entity aims to establish a sustainable space for film education, training and production in Gaza, “while connecting emerging Palestinian filmmakers with the wider international film community,” as a statement put it.

	The Gaza Cinema Academy is being supported by 2025 Venice Silver Lion winner — and Venice jury member — Kaouther Ben Hania (“The Voice of Hind Rajab”) and fellow directors Annemarie Jacir (“Palestine 36″), Mai Masri (“3000 Nights”) — who is the academy’s co-founder — and Ezzaldeen Shalah, as well as actors Hiam Abbas, Ramy Youssef and Saleh Bakri. Italian producer Graziella Bildesheim and Cairo-based distributor and Arab film industry promoter Alaa Karkouti are also on board.
	

	The academy will focus “on film education and training, supporting young talent and women, developing and producing new Palestinian films, strengthening the presence of filmmakers in Gaza and their connections with the Palestinian, Arab and international film communities, and building a sustainable film institution in the Gaza Strip,” the statement said.


	They are seeking to build a rapport with film festivals and other cultural institutions, as well as film funds, and production companies. “The academy aspires to build an international network of partners that supports emerging film talent in Gaza, strengthens opportunities for learning and production, and helps their films reach festivals, platforms and audiences around the world,” it noted. 
	

	“In Gaza, cinema is not merely an art form; it is a means of preserving memory, reclaiming our right to shape our own image, and giving a new generation the tools to tell its own story,” said Shalah, who is founder of the Gaza International Women’s Film Festival and co-founder of the Gaza Cinema Academy, in the statement. “We want the academy to open a window for young people and women in Gaza to learn, create and make their own films, and for their voices and images to reach the world. We invite our partners in institutions, universities and the international film community to be part of building this space.“

	The first edition of the Gaza International Women’s Film Festival was held Oct. 26-31, 2025, amid rubble in the heart of the Gaza strip. The Gaza fest opened with “The Voice of Hind Rajab.”

	There are two Palestinian films in Venice’s official selection this year: Ahmed Hassouna’s “Citizen Osama,” which portrays a photographer (film still above) as he attempts to juggle his roles as father and a journalist while capturing the realities of war in Gaza; and Muayad Alayan’s “Conversation With the Sea,” about a 60-year-old Palestinian man named Kamal who becomes entangled in a tendentious web of Israeli bureaucracy.

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Nathan Fielder’s Documentary About Elizabeth Holmes Is a Shameless, Fascinating, Reality-TV-Eats-Its-Tale Look at Entitled Duplicity
description: In a world where Lindsay Clancy can inspire an onslaught of sympathetic voyeuristic fascination, why not Elizabeth Holmes? Earlier tonight, the scre
body:
In a world where Lindsay Clancy can inspire an onslaught of sympathetic voyeuristic fascination, why not Elizabeth Holmes? Earlier tonight, the screening of an unannounced mystery movie at the Telluride Film Festival generated every bit as much pre-screening buzz as any of the major titles programmed here. And when the movie was revealed to be “You Can See Everything,” a 174-minute documentary, co-directed by the cult comedian Nathan Fielder, about Elizabeth Holmes, the former CEO of Theranos who is now serving an 11-year prison sentence after being convicted of defrauding her investors, the sensation of “WTF? I’ve got to watch this!” did not subside as the movie went on. It only intensified.
	

	“You Can See Everything” is just about the furthest thing from a “pure” documentary you’ve ever seen. That’s part of its appeal — it’s a one-of-a-kind reality-TV-as-hangout-movie psychodrama circus. Yet it’s been made with a spirit of true inquiry, driven by Fielder’s acidly quizzical personality (as an onscreen interviewer, he’s got the most drop-dead deadpan since Steven Wright), and it gets its hooks in you.


	Fielder isn’t here to throw open the question of Elizabeth Holmes’ guilt. He wants to know what made her tick. But why, you may ask, is the comedian behind shows like “The Curse” and “The Rehearsal” making a three-hour movie about the woman who became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire by convincing the world that she’d created a revolutionary new means of blood testing? Holmes, after her conviction, stayed out of the public eye, but shortly before her prison sentence was set to begin she decided she wanted someone to document her last days of freedom. Maybe she wanted to have her say?
	

	Whatever the motivation, Fielder, who has often operated in a nether zone between fiction and reality, was looking for a project to collaborate on with Lance Oppenheim, a documentarian he’d become friendly with. And so, with the support of A24, and without quite knowing what they were after (or, by their own admission, what the hell they were doing), the two of them stepped into the breach. Thirty-five days before the start of Holmes’ prison sentence, in 2023, they brought a camera crew to the spacious wood-paneled beachside home in Del Mar where she was living with her partner, the California hotel heir Billy Evans, and their two children (including an infant daughter). Fielder was there to hang out, observe, and interview Holmes, trying to get inside her head. That proved to be a weirder and wilder journey than anyone might have expected.

	The Elizabeth Holmes we see has a winsome soft presence, with a Cupid’s-bow grin and eyes that beam without blinking too much. She resembles the ’80s and ’90s actress Kim Greist, and has a manner that’s disarming in its gentleness. Yet when Fielder asks about the crimes she was convicted of, she pleads a strange kind of ignorance. She claims she did nothing wrong, and it’s clear she believes it. But how is that possible?

	In 2015, Holmes had become a celebrity entrepreneur, based on the $9 billion valuation of her health technology company, Theranos — a company that turned out to have been built on a complete scam. For a brief time, Holmes convinced the world that she’d developed a revolutionary device for blood testing that required very small volumes of blood, such as the amount you’d get from a pinprick. She convinced top-drawer investors (including Rupert Murdoch and Larry Ellison) to pour millions of dollars into the company. For credibility, she assembled a board of directors that included such ancient luminaries as George P. Shultz, Henry Kissinger, and James Mattis. There was only one problem: the “revolutionary” technology didn’t exist.

	Numerous experts, starting with the Stanford medical professor Phyllis Gardner, told Holmes that her idea wouldn’t work; you couldn’t mine voluminous amounts of data from just a few droplets of blood. But Holmes, along with her business partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani (who was also her romantic partner), sold the deception anyway. For a short while they were quite “successful” at it, though in hindsight it’s clear that the castle in the air they built — all spun out of the trendy idea that medical science could be democratized — was destined to crash and burn. Because it was all made up! Holmes had spun the pinprick idea out of her own fear of needles. This was her fantasy, elevated into an invention that didn’t actually exist.
	

	So how can she defend herself now? What she tells Fielder, with an implacable conviction that suggests a belief in her own narrative that’s nothing short of monomaniacal, is that the device patented by Theranos, which she sold as “the iPod of health care,” could, in fact, host any blood test that existed. The only thing they hadn’t quite worked out was the chemistry that would go into the tests. In other words, the device was based on the projection of a technology that didn’t exist yet. But the more Holmes talks to Fielder, the more he teases out her unhinged rationale, which is: The device works fine! We just had to figure out that pesky chemistry stuff! The strange thing is that Holmes has such a corporate mindset that she treats the chemistry stuff…that hadn’t been invented yet…as just another glitchy small problem that could easily be solved. (Have the solution on my desk Monday morning!) 

	She believes her version of reality. Fielder, who is not taken in by any of this (his questions remain rigorous in their skepticism), at one point gives vent to his impish side by showing Elizabeth and Billy the famous Abbott and Costello routine “Who’s on First?” When it ends, he tries to get Holmes to explain what the joke is (that “Who” is the first baseman’s name, but the name sounds like a question — hence the routine’s glorious verbal slapstick). And she can’t do it; she can’t grasp the joke. It’s not just that she lacks a sense of humor (though frankly, she kind of does). It’s that she’s got the malignant narcissist’s need to have words mean only what she decrees them to mean. She can’t hear any other meaning. Hence: her device did “work,” and still does (it can run any test!). That’s why she and Bobby, years after her conviction, are still pitching Theranos to other investors (as if anyone would go near her). This is a highly rarefied level of delusional thinking.

	Holmes says to Fielder that she’s never told a lie in her life. Her whole vibe is “sincerity.” (Though it’s also one of passive-aggressive unbroken-eye-contact creepiness.) The lesson of her legal case isn’t just that she was found guilty of defrauding investors, but that her faulty device, had it been put on the market, would have hurt people. That’s why the real question “You Can See Everything” is asking isn’t: Is she guilty? Rather, it’s: What makes people like Elizabeth Holmes tick? (And how many of them are out there?) Fielder and Elizabeth and Bobby sit down to watch the 2022 Hulu miniseries “The Dropout,” which was based on the case, with Amanda Seyfried giving a pointed performance as Holmes. Holmes suggests that the series is a TV-movie crock. But is it?  
	

	The documentary’s first half ends with Holmes saying goodbye to her family and going off to the minimum-security Bryan Prison in Texas. The prison won’t allow anyone to interview her, so that’s more or less the last we’ll see of her. And we’ve pretty much gotten the skinny on her, which is that she has a brick wall standing between herself and the truth, and an indifference to the harm she might have caused, that borders on the sociopathic. So what is there left to discover?

	Plenty, it turns out. With Holmes out of the picture, Fielder needs someone to sustain her presence. So he calls Amanda Seyfried, who sits and watches the scene we’ve just seen of Holmes sitting and watching Seyfried portray her. Are you feeling the meta of it all? That sounds gimmicky, but as the documentary goes on, and Fielder creates transcripts of things that Holmes has spoken (including a phone chat he has with her in prison), who better to read the transcripts — to turn this reality into theater, and by doing so to turn it back into reality — than Amanda Seyfried? She gives an increasingly accurate performance as Holmes, getting inside her head, to the point that Seyfried starts to sympathize with her, at least when it comes to what a glowering aggro control freak Holmes’ partner Bobby is. As Bobby continues to make himself accessible to the filmmakers, exposing his dark side at every turn, I was afraid the movie might use him to create a kind of toxic excuse for what Holmes did.

	But part of the jaunty power of “You Can See Everything” is that the film never mounts an apologia for Elizabeth Holmes. Bobby may be repugnant in his cockiness, and in the way he takes control of Holmes’ image, allowing the iconic photograph of her making the “OK” sign to be used on billboards, tweeting out hostile tweets under her name, and striking a deal with the A24 executives — yes, there’s a meeting with them in the movie, at which point we’re either in meta heaven or hell — that will give him some of the profits from the movie. Does Holmes know about the deal? No. But she claims to want it that way. Her grand assertion is that she never cared about the money. And yet the money — the value of her company — became the very core of her identity. “You Can See Everything” overlaps reality, performance, deception, and mental illness, and by the end it brings you to the enigmatic space where every one of those things meet.

schema.headline: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Nathan Fielder’s Documentary About Elizabeth Holmes Is a Shameless, Fascinating, Reality-TV-Eats-Its-Tale Look at Entitled Duplicity

title: French Drama Series ‘The Red and the Black’: Passion, Power, Political Intrigue and Victor Belmondo’s Anti-Romantic Hero
description: “The Red and the Black,” an adaptation of Stendhal’s 1830 novel, follows the young Julien Sorel (Victor Belmondo) as he pursues greatness, rising so
body:
“The Red and the Black,” an adaptation of Stendhal’s 1830 novel, follows the young Julien Sorel (Victor Belmondo) as he pursues greatness, rising socially beyond his modest upbringing while entangled in a web of passion, power and political intrigue.

	Following screenings at Canneseries and the Italian Global Series Festival, “The Red and the Black,” produced by Siècle Productions for France Télévisions, makes its international market debut at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, where it’s being sold by Wild Bunch.
	

	The four-part series is directed by Gaël Morel, who reunites with Belmondo following their acclaimed 2024 relationship drama “To Live, to Die, to Live Again,” and written by Georges-Marc Benamou and Gilles Taurand, whose previous collaborations include “The Last Mitterrand” and more recently “The Plague.”




	

									Credit: Nicolas Velter/France Télévisions/Siècle Productions/Wild Bunch
	



	The creators found inspiration in the enduring qualities of Stendhal’s work.

	“There is a universality to great literature, particularly 19th century French and Anglo-Saxon literature, from Stendhal to Jane Austen, who was almost Stendhal’s contemporary,” Benamou tells Variety.

	“We can see young audiences going to cinemas to watch these adaptations again. It is literature of intense passions: free in its tone, its depiction of love, and its drama, yet often avoiding romantic sentimentality. In Stendhal’s case, Julien Sorel, the protagonist, is precisely an anti-romantic hero: an ambitious man whose aspirations are thwarted. That is what makes him both compelling and tragic.”

	The story of an ambitious and calculating young man of modest origins trying to establish himself in circles of power dominated by ruthless and manipulative actors and confronted by great moral hypocrisy could very well be a tale of the 21st century.
	

	The renowned work’s timeless themes have led to several big and small-screen adaptations over the decades, including Claude Autant-Lara’s 1954 version starring Gérard Philipe and the 1993 BBC series featuring Ewan McGregor in one of his earliest roles.

	“There are indeed parallels with the present day,” Benamou adds. “This is part of the genius, and, once again, the universal appeal, of a great writer such as Stendhal, who was a dissenting voice in his own time.

	“The parallels are clear: the return of moral conservatism, embodied by the Congregation of Catholic fundamentalists determined to destroy Julien Sorel; women constrained by society who choose to emancipate themselves; and the social determinism faced by this class defector, who is unable to escape his background. All of this, the resurgence of moral conservatism, stalled social mobility, and women’s emancipation, still resonates today in France, Europe and America.”

	Morel stresses that the series “speaks more directly to contemporary issues: class defection, social determinism, and male–female relationships, which are especially modern in this work.

	“Julien Sorel rises through society thanks to women, because they embody power. I think that the theme of class defection is at the heart of the modernity. Someone like Julien Sorel, struggling to rise through society, raises questions that remain very relevant in France today, particularly when we speak of social mobility, which may be even more stuck now than it was then.

	“Unfortunately, it is a theme that remains contemporary and is likely to do so for a long time. Several of its themes therefore resonate with current events. There is also the return of obscurantism, embodied by the ‘black’ in the title.”

	While enthusiastically embracing the material and its enduring themes, the production team faced a major task in transposing such a rich and complex novel into a television series.  

	“The abundance of characters, settings, social classes and novelistic digressions made this a challenging work to adapt,” Morel explains.

	“So, I would describe it as a variation on the novel rather than a faithful adaptation. Our aim was to focus on several aspects of the story and draw from them a clear, coherent storyline.
	

	“The themes we chose to foreground strike me as remarkably contemporary. Gilles Taurand and Georges-Marc Benamou’s clever work, applying the conventions of serial storytelling to this variation, has given the work a much-needed ‘rejuvenation’ while remaining deeply faithful to its spirit.”

	In casting “The Red and the Black,” the production team found their ideal lead in Belmondo, particularly for their more authentic take on the character of Julien Sorel. The cast also includes Camille Razat (“Emily in Paris”) and Virginie Ledoyen (“At Work”).

	“Victor Belmondo’s great strength lies in the fact that he is an outstanding young actor who has developed a relationship of friendship and trust with director Gaël Morel,” Benamou notes. “This is their second film together, and Gaël and I felt that, with Victor, we wanted to find an ‘anti-Gérard Philipe.’ The distinctly romantic image associated with Claude Autant-Lara’s 1954 film has, to some extent, overshadowed Stendhal’s work. We wanted to return to the origins of Julien Sorel: a man whose ambition is thwarted both by his own limitations and by those imposed by others, an anti-romantic hero.”

	Morel adds: “Victor Belmondo immediately struck me as the ideal Julien Sorel. His youthfulness and intensity, together with his ability to convey a brooding, determined quality, provide the perfect vehicle for capturing the essence of the character.

	“Sorel is not a romantic hero, although he may adopt that persona to seduce. Behind his youth and impoverished social background lies a fierce ambition and an almost pathological need for recognition. This interpretation of the character, as a calculating, seductive, boastful young man who sees life as a conquest, seems to me the most accurate. It is far removed from the romantic, victim-like figure that has sometimes been presented in earlier adaptations.”

	For Wild Bunch, “The Red and the Black” epitomizes what it sees as ideal content. 

	“While brand recognition is important, our ambition goes further: to develop a deep understanding of the constantly evolving needs of our international buyers and propose programs that deliver strong audience appeal while bringing families together around a shared story,” says Diana Bartha, head of international sales and acquisitions at Wild Bunch.
	

	“‘The Red and the Black’ ticks all the boxes. Universal and modern, it appeals to audiences across generations and offers the familiarity of a well-established concept alongside a fresh, contemporary take. Its broad appeal, strong emotional connection and ability to unite viewers make it the ideal series for this season — one that needs no introduction.”

title: Egyptian TV Host Sentenced to Death by Hanging in Drug Trafficking Case
description:
Egyptian TV Host
                          Sentenced to Death by Hanging for Drug Trafficking
body:
Egyptian TV Host
                          Sentenced to Death by Hanging for Drug Trafficking
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Egyptian TV host broke down in tears in court after learning her fate in a massive drug trafficking case ... death by hanging.
      
    
            Sarah Khalifa, a 39-year-old former host of the Egyptian crime show "Mission Impossible," was sentenced to death in Cairo after being convicted of helping run an organized drug operation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She and 11 others were sentenced to death after prosecutors accused the group of importing raw materials used to manufacture synthetic drugs and storing the finished product inside residential homes.
      

            Khalifa reportedly sobbed as the sentence was handed down, pleading with the court and insisting she didn't need money from drugs. She denies the allegations, reportedly telling investigators she'd never even smoked a cigarette.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Authorities say the sprawling case involved 28 defendants and led to the seizure of more than 1,600 pounds of narcotics, along with unlicensed guns and ammunition.
      
    
            Nine other defendants were sentenced to life in prison, while seven were acquitted.
      
    
            Khalifa -- who also ran a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event-planning company -- was arrested in 2025.
      
    
            The death sentence was issued after the court consulted Egypt's grand mufti, a required step in Egyptian capital cases ... and the ruling can still be appealed.

title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool a Mess Again After D.C. Storms
description:
Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
                          One Mess After Another Since Makeover
body:
Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
                          One Mess After Another Since Makeover
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is looking rough again ... after powerful storms turned the already-troubled tourist attraction into an even bigger mess.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Fencing and black tarp surrounding the closed-off pool have toppled over, mucking up the view ... with parts of the barrier spilling into the water and leaving the area looking battered and disheveled.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Recent storms hammered D.C. with heavy rain and powerful winds ... knocking down trees and sending debris flying across the District -- and the Reflecting Pool wasn't spared.
      

            Of course, it's just the latest headache for the famous landmark after its multimillion-dollar makeover became a months-long saga.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... the pool developed algae and its new blue coating began peeling shortly after the renovation. President Donald Trump blamed vandals for some of the damage, leading to arrests -- but prosecutors later dropped the felony case against former Olympian David Hearn after concluding the installation itself was flawed.
      
    
            Trump has continued insisting vandalism played a role ... and the administration recently shelled out more millions to tackle the pool's algae problem.
      
    
            So much for keeping up appearances ...
